# The Space Between Thoughts

I'm thinking about how we rarely notice the moment something becomes familiar. There's no bell that rings. No announcement. One day you're struggling to remember someone's name, and the next day you can't imagine not knowing it. The transition happens in the dark, while we're looking elsewhere.

I've been sitting at this desk for three years now. I know where the light hits the wood grain at 4 PM. I know which floorboard creaks if you step too far to the left. I know the sound my chair makes when I lean back—that particular squeak that means I'm stuck on something. But I couldn't tell you when this place stopped feeling new. It just did.

There's something about attention that fascinates me. We think we see everything we look at, but we're mostly looking at the narrow slice of the world we expect to see. A psychologist once showed people a video of basketball players and asked them to count passes. Most people missed the gorilla walking across the court in a full costume. A gorilla! How do you miss that? The answer is simple: they weren't looking for it. Their attention was a spotlight, and the gorilla was standing just outside the beam.

I wonder how many gorillas have walked across my own life while I was counting something else.

My neighbor plays the same song most mornings around 7 AM. It's a classical piece—violin, I think. Probably Vivaldi, though I'm not certain. I've heard it maybe two hundred times. Two hundred times, and I still couldn't hum it back to you. But I notice when they skip a morning. The silence is louder than the music ever was. Absence is like that. It takes up more room than presence.

There's a coffee shop three blocks away that has the best coffee I've ever tasted. I go there on Thursday mornings. It's terrible for my budget and probably my blood pressure, but Thursday mornings aren't about budget or blood pressure. They're about sitting in the corner by the window and watching people who are in a hurry. Nobody sits in my corner. It's apparently the kind of spot people don't notice, which is exactly why I like it.

I've been reading the same book for six months. Not because it's long—it's only 240 pages—but because I keep getting distracted by my own thoughts and then going back to reread paragraphs. I can't remember what happens in it anymore. I probably never will. But I love the way it smells like old paper and dust, and I love that I can open it to any page and find something I don't remember reading.

My mother called last week. She wanted to know why I don't visit. I didn't have a good answer. I told her I've been busy, which is true but not the actual reason. The actual reason is harder to explain. It's something about how time works differently when you're somewhere you haven't lived in years. In my childhood home, I'm always seeing the person I used to be in the corners. I'm always comparing the present to the past. It's exhausting.

But I didn't tell her that. I said I'd visit soon and probably meant it.

I've started noticing birds lately. There's one that comes to the fire escape outside my window. I don't know what kind it is. It's gray and small and has an urgent way of moving, like it's late for something. I named it Wednesday because it seems to visit on Wednesdays, though I'm not entirely sure I'm tracking the days correctly. I put out breadcrumbs, but Wednesday doesn't eat them. It just looks at them with what I imagine is disdain and then flies away. We have this relationship now, Wednesday and I. It's not affectionate, but it's consistent.

I read somewhere that the average person has about 70,000 thoughts per day. Seventy thousand. That seems like too many and not nearly enough at the same time. Most of them are probably repetitions of thoughts we've already had. The mind is a very small room that we traverse over and over, looking at the same corners, touching the same walls, expecting something to have changed.

I want to do something significant. Something that matters. But I don't know what that means anymore. When I was younger, significance seemed clearer. You became a doctor or wrote a book or changed something. Now I think maybe significance is quieter. Maybe it's in the Thursday mornings at the coffee shop, or in noticing that Wednesday the bird didn't come last week, or in rereading the same paragraph four times because you were thinking about something else.

Maybe it's in this moment, writing words that I'll probably never read again, that no one else will read, that exist solely because I needed to put something into the world today.

The light is leaving my desk now. It's almost 5 PM. Tomorrow it will do the same thing, and the day after that, and I'll keep sitting here counting passes, missing gorillas, listening to absence, and probably never actually finishing that book.

But Wednesday might come back. The coffee will still taste good on Thursday. My mother will probably call again, and I'll probably still not visit. The floorboard will creak. The chair will squeak. The song will play.

And that's okay. That's enough. That has to be enough.

We live in the space between the moments we think matter, and that's where everything actually happens.
